title: Fertilisers, medicines, fuels and paints: how chemistry makes them, and why the amount matters

summary.text: The nitrogen in a bag of urea fertiliser was taken from the air. The gas in an LPG cylinder and the wax of a candle both came from crude oil. Chemical factories change a few raw materials into fertilisers, medicines, fuels and paints. The raw materials are air, water, rocks, crude oil and living beings. Each of these products helps in the right amount and harms in too large an amount. Your child mixes three paints to find what keeps colour on a surface. They also give the same drops of colour to a small glass and a big pot. This shows why a child's dose of medicine is smaller.
summary.art: A white sack of urea fertiliser standing in a paddy field, with a dotted arrow drawn from the open sky down into the sack.

intro.hook: A farmer's urea, a paracetamol tablet, the gas in a cylinder and the paint on a wall look nothing alike. Where does each of them come from?
intro.text: None of the four is dug up or picked ready to use. People make each one by chemical reactions, starting from air, rock, crude oil or a plant. In this unit you find a fuel, a medicine, a paint and a plant food in your own home. You mix three paints and test which one stays on. You line up things made from crude oil, from cooking gas to candle wax. You also test why the same dose is weak in a big body and strong in a small one.
intro.art: Four things side by side on a kitchen counter: a small sack of white urea grains, a strip of tablets, an LPG cylinder and an open tin of blue paint with a brush.

outcomes: I can say where fertilisers, medicines, fuels and paints come from: raw materials changed by chemical reactions.
I can name the three main nutrients in fertiliser, and say what happens when a field gets too much.
I can explain what a fuel is, where LPG and petrol come from, and what burning them makes.
I can say what a medicine is, name two from plants or moulds, and say why medicines are tested.
I can explain why the dose matters, and why a child's dose is smaller than a grown-up's.
I can name the three parts of a paint, and test what the binder does.
I can explain what by-products and pollution are, and give one way that factories cut harm.
I can tell how people found out that substances from living bodies can be made in a laboratory.

terms.meaning: A substance taken from nature that a factory starts with.
terms.example: Air, water, rock, crude oil and plants are raw materials.
terms.art: Five small pictures in a row: a cloud, a water drop, a lump of rock, a barrel of dark oil and a green plant.

terms.meaning: The useful substance that a factory sets out to make.
terms.example: Urea is the product of a urea factory.
terms.art: A factory building with an arrow leading out to a neat stack of filled sacks.

terms.meaning: Another substance that is made at the same time as the product. Some by-products are useful, and some are waste.
terms.example: Making hydrogen from natural gas also makes carbon dioxide, as a by-product.
terms.art: A factory with one large arrow leading to sacks and a smaller side arrow leading to a cloud of gas.

terms.meaning: All the factories that make new substances by chemical reactions.
terms.example: A refinery in Kochi and a medicine factory in Hyderabad are both part of the chemical industry.
terms.art: A row of factory buildings with tall towers, round tanks and pipes running between them.

terms.meaning: A substance added to soil to give plants the nutrients they need.
terms.example: A farmer near Thanjavur spreads urea on her paddy field.
terms.art: A woman farmer scattering white grains by hand over young green paddy plants.

terms.meaning: A substance that a living being must take in to live and grow. The three main plant nutrients in fertiliser are nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
terms.example: The letters N, P and K on a fertiliser bag stand for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
terms.art: A fertiliser bag with the large letters N, P and K printed on it and three numbers below them.

terms.meaning: A white solid that is rich in nitrogen. It is the most used nitrogen fertiliser in India. Your own body also makes urea, and it leaves in your urine.
terms.example: A 45 kilogram bag of urea holds about 21 kilograms of nitrogen.
terms.art: A handful of small white round grains on an open palm.

terms.meaning: A substance that gives out heat when it burns.
terms.example: LPG, petrol, firewood and candle wax are all fuels.
terms.art: A blue flame on a gas stove burner under a steel pot.

terms.meaning: A thick, dark liquid found deep under the ground or the sea bed. It is a mixture of many substances.
terms.example: Crude oil is pumped from under the sea off Mumbai.
terms.art: An oil platform standing in the sea, with a pipe drawn going down through the sea bed to a dark pool of oil.

terms.meaning: A substance whose molecules are made only of hydrogen atoms and carbon atoms.
terms.example: Each molecule of propane, in LPG, has 3 carbon atoms and 8 hydrogen atoms.
terms.art: A short chain of three large black balls with eight small white balls attached around them.

terms.meaning: A factory that separates crude oil into its useful parts.
terms.example: The refinery at Digboi in Assam has worked since 1901.
terms.art: A tall steel tower with pipes coming out at different heights, beside round storage tanks.

terms.meaning: A substance that prevents an illness, treats it or eases its signs.
terms.art: A strip of white tablets and a small bottle of syrup with a measuring cap.

terms.meaning: The amount of a medicine taken at one time.
terms.example: A label gives a smaller dose for a child than for a grown-up.
terms.art: Two measuring caps side by side, one filled to a low line and one filled to a high line.

terms.meaning: A fine coloured powder that does not dissolve. It gives a paint its colour.
terms.example: Red ochre is a pigment made from a soft red rock.
terms.art: Three small heaps of fine powder, one red, one yellow and one white, on a stone slab.

terms.meaning: The part of a paint that holds the pigment together and sticks it to the surface.
terms.example: In Three Paints, white glue is the binder that keeps the colour powder on the card.
terms.art: A magnified view of coloured grains held inside a clear layer on top of a wall.

terms.meaning: The liquid in a paint that makes it thin enough to spread. It evaporates as the paint dries.
terms.example: Water is the solvent in most wall paint.
terms.art: A wet painted wall with small wavy arrows rising from it into the air.

explanations.concept: Where fertilisers, medicines, fuels and paints come from
explanations.definition: The chemical industry takes a few raw materials from nature. It changes them, by chemical reactions, into substances that people use.
explanations.description: A chemical reaction changes substances into new substances. The atoms stay the same, and they join up in a new way. A chemical factory does this in very large amounts. It starts with raw materials. There are only a few kinds: air, water, rocks and salts, crude oil and natural gas, and living beings such as plants and moulds. The substance the factory sets out to make is its product. Most reactions also make other substances, called by-products. A factory needs energy too, and most of that energy still comes from burning fuel. Four families of products are in this unit. Fertilisers feed crops. Medicines treat illness. Fuels give energy. Paints colour and protect surfaces. Each one reaches your home after many steps. The paracetamol in a tablet is made in a few reactions from a substance called phenol. Phenol itself is made from crude oil.
examples: The nitrogen in urea comes from the air.
The white pigment in wall paint is made from a black beach sand.
LPG is separated from crude oil and natural gas.
explanations.art: A chart with five raw materials on the left, a factory in the middle, and a fertiliser sack, a tablet strip, a gas cylinder and a paint tin on the right.

explanations.concept: Fertilisers: putting back what the harvest takes away
explanations.definition: A fertiliser is a substance added to soil to supply nutrients that plants need. The three main nutrients are nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
explanations.description: A plant makes sugar from air, water and sunlight. To build leaves, roots and seeds, she also needs nutrients from the soil. She needs nitrogen most of all, and then phosphorus and potassium. Their chemical symbols are N, P and K. When a crop is harvested, the nutrients inside the crop leave the field. A field that is harvested year after year grows poorer, unless something puts the nutrients back. Dung, compost and bean crops put some back. Fertilisers from factories put back more, and quickly. Urea supplies nitrogen. In every 100 kilograms of urea there are 46 kilograms of nitrogen. Phosphorus fertiliser is made from phosphate rock, which is mined at Jhamarkotra in Rajasthan. Potassium fertiliser is called potash. It is mined from the salts of ancient seas that dried up. India buys nearly all its potash from other countries. A fertiliser bag often carries three numbers, such as 19:19:19. They show how rich the fertiliser is in N, P and K, in that order.
examples: A 45 kilogram bag of urea holds about 21 kilograms of nitrogen.
A bag marked 0:0:60 holds potash, with no nitrogen and no phosphorus.
Since 2015, urea sold to farmers in India is coated with neem oil. The coating slows the release of nitrogen in the soil.
explanations.art: A paddy field with a cart carrying sacks of harvested grain away, and a farmer adding white grains back to the soil.

explanations.concept: Nitrogen: from the air to the field
explanations.definition: Air is about four fifths nitrogen gas, but plants cannot use nitrogen in that form. Factories join it with hydrogen to make ammonia, and ammonia is made into urea.
explanations.description: Nitrogen is all around every plant. In every 100 litres of air, about 78 litres are nitrogen gas. But the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule hold each other very tightly. A plant has no way to pull them apart. Some bacteria can pull them apart, such as those who live in the root swellings of beans. Lightning can too. In 1909 the German chemist Fritz Haber found a way to do it in a laboratory. He pressed nitrogen and hydrogen together, very hot, over a metal catalyst. A catalyst is a helper that speeds up a reaction and is not used up. The two gases joined to make ammonia. By 1913 the engineer Carl Bosch had built a factory that did this in huge amounts. Today the hydrogen comes mostly from natural gas and steam. The ammonia is then joined with carbon dioxide to make urea. Scientists estimate that food grown with this nitrogen feeds about half the people on Earth. Making it uses a great deal of fuel.
examples: The protein in a grain of wheat holds nitrogen that may have been in the air one year earlier.
Beans, peas and groundnuts get nitrogen from bacteria in their root swellings.
A flash of lightning joins a little nitrogen with oxygen, and rain carries it to the soil.
explanations.art: An arrow path from a blue sky, through a factory with a tall steel vessel, to a sack of white grains, to a field of wheat.

explanations.definition: A fuel is a substance that gives out heat when it burns. Most fuels used today come from crude oil, natural gas and coal.
explanations.description: Crude oil formed from tiny living beings of the sea who died many millions of years ago. Mud buried them. Heat and pressure slowly changed their remains into oil and gas. Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons. A hydrocarbon molecule is a chain of carbon atoms with hydrogen atoms attached. Some chains are short and some are long. A refinery separates them by boiling. It heats the crude oil, and the vapours rise up a tall tower. Short chains boil at low temperatures, and they are collected near the top. Long chains are collected lower down. The shortest chains have 3 or 4 carbon atoms. They make LPG, the cooking gas. Petrol has chains of about 5 to 12 carbon atoms. Diesel has about 12 to 20. Candle wax has about 20 to 40. The thickest part is bitumen, the black tar that binds a road. The longer the chain, the thicker the substance is and the harder it is to boil. Refineries also supply the starting substances for plastics, paints and many medicines.
examples: The refinery at Jamnagar in Gujarat is the largest in the world.
LPG has no smell of its own. A strong-smelling substance is added so that people notice a leak.
Petroleum jelly and candle wax are both made from crude oil.
explanations.art: A tall refinery tower cut open, with pipes at five heights labelled from top to bottom: LPG, petrol, diesel, wax and bitumen.

explanations.definition: When a hydrocarbon fuel burns, it joins with oxygen from the air. The reaction makes carbon dioxide and water, and it gives out heat.
explanations.description: Burning is a chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen. The carbon atoms of the fuel join with oxygen and become carbon dioxide. The hydrogen atoms join with oxygen and become water vapour. No atom is lost. Burning 1 kilogram of LPG makes about 3 kilograms of carbon dioxide, because oxygen from the air has been added. A flame that gets too little air also makes soot and a poisonous gas called carbon monoxide. Carbon dioxide is not poisonous in small amounts. You breathe it out, and plants take it in. But carbon dioxide holds heat in the air. In 1856 the American scientist Eunice Foote filled glass tubes with different gases and stood them in the sun. The tube of carbon dioxide grew the hottest. She wrote that more of this gas in the air would make the Earth warmer. People now burn so much fuel that this is happening. So chemists work on fuels that add less carbon dioxide. Biogas is made by microbes from dung and food waste. Ethanol is made from sugarcane, and in India it is mixed into petrol. Hydrogen burns to give only water.
examples: A cold steel plate held above a candle flame mists over with water and turns black with soot.
A yellow, smoky stove flame is getting too little air. A blue flame is burning cleanly.
A full home cylinder holds 14.2 kilograms of LPG. Burning all of it makes about 43 kilograms of carbon dioxide.
explanations.art: A gas flame with a chain of carbon and hydrogen balls entering from below, oxygen pairs entering from the sides, and carbon dioxide and water molecules leaving at the top.

explanations.concept: Medicines: substances that change how a body works
explanations.definition: A medicine is a substance that prevents an illness, treats it or eases its signs. It works by joining to particular molecules in the body or in a germ.
explanations.description: Many medicines were first found in other living beings. Willow bark eases pain, and chemists made aspirin from the substance in the bark. The bark of the cinchona tree holds quinine, which treats malaria. In 1928 Alexander Fleming saw that bacteria died near a mould called Penicillium. That mould gave us penicillin. In 1972 Tu Youyou and her team in China drew a malaria medicine, artemisinin, out of the sweet wormwood plant. She had read in an old Chinese book that the plant should be soaked in cold water. So she stopped boiling the plant, and the medicine was no longer destroyed. In India, Asima Chatterjee studied the chemistry of medicinal plants for about fifty years. Once chemists know which molecule does the work, a factory can make that molecule. A factory can also change the molecule a little, to make it stronger or safer. Yellapragada Subbarow, born in Andhra Pradesh, led teams that made medicines for cancer and for filaria. A new medicine is tested for years, first in a laboratory and then on thousands of volunteers. Most new medicines fail these tests. India's factories make a large share of the world's low-cost medicines and vaccines.
examples: Quinine was once grown for India in cinchona plantations in the Nilgiri hills.
A medicine for childhood blood cancer comes from the periwinkle plant, called nithyakalyani in Tamil.
Chalky antacid tablets are made from limestone, a rock.
explanations.art: A piece of tree bark, a dish of blue-green mould and a leafy wormwood plant on the left, with arrows to a strip of tablets on the right.

explanations.concept: The dose: why the amount decides
explanations.definition: The dose is the amount of a medicine taken at one time. Too small a dose does nothing, the right dose helps, and too large a dose harms.
explanations.description: A medicine spreads through the blood and the water of the body. A bigger body has more blood and water, so the same amount is spread thinner. That is why a dose is often worked out from body mass. A label may give so many milligrams for each kilogram. A child's body is smaller than a grown-up's, so a child's dose is smaller. A child's liver and kidneys also handle some medicines differently. So only the label or a doctor decides a child's dose. The same rule of amount holds outside medicine. Your body needs salt, yet a few large spoonfuls eaten at once can make a person very ill. About 500 years ago a Swiss doctor called Paracelsus put the rule in one line. Everything is a poison, he wrote, and only the dose makes a thing not a poison. Fertiliser follows the rule too. A little feeds a plant. Too much draws water out of the roots, and the rest washes into ponds and rivers.
examples: A syrup for children and a tablet for grown-ups may hold the same medicine in different amounts.
One spoon of plant food in a bucket of water feeds pot plants. One spoon in a cup of water can burn their roots.
A little carbon dioxide in the air keeps the Earth warm enough to live on. More makes the Earth too warm.
explanations.art: Three glasses of water in a row with one drop, three drops and many drops of colour, labelled too little, right and too much.

explanations.definition: A paint is a mixture of three main parts. The pigment gives the colour. The binder holds the pigment and sticks it to the surface. The solvent makes the paint thin enough to spread.
explanations.description: A pigment is a fine coloured powder that does not dissolve. The oldest pigments are coloured earths. Thousands of years ago, people painted the rock shelters of Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh with red ochre. Red ochre is a soft rock coloured by iron oxide, the same substance as rust. Today the most used pigment is a white one, titanium dioxide. It is made from a black sand that is mined on the beaches of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. A pigment alone is only dust, and it falls off when it dries. The binder is what makes a paint stay. In the caves of Ajanta, the painters mixed their pigments with glue. Lac is a resin made by tiny lac insects. It binds the colours on the wooden toys of Channapatna. In most wall paint today the binder is a kind of plastic made from crude oil. The solvent is the liquid that carries the pigment and the binder. In water-based paint the solvent is water. Some paints use other liquids, such as turpentine, which have a strong smell. A paint also protects. A coat of paint keeps air and water away from steel, so the steel does not rust.
examples: A chalk line on a slate rubs off, because chalk has pigment and no binder.
A wax crayon line stays, because the wax binds the pigment.
The red on a Channapatna toy does not come off on your hands, because lac holds it.
explanations.art: A magnified slice of wet paint on a wall, showing coloured grains, a clear sticky binder around them and wavy lines of solvent.

explanations.definition: A wet paint becomes a hard coat in one of three ways. Its solvent evaporates, or its binder reacts with a gas in the air, or it cools.
explanations.description: Water-based wall paint holds its binder as tiny particles of plastic floating in water. As the water evaporates, the particles are pressed together and join into one thin sheet. The sheet traps the pigment. Once the sheet has formed, water no longer dissolves it. Oil paint hardens in another way. Its binder is an oil, such as linseed oil, that reacts with oxygen from the air. The oil molecules link to each other and form a tough solid. This is a chemical reaction, so oil paint goes on hardening after it feels dry. Lime wash is the white chuna on many older walls. It hardens by a reaction too. Lime takes in carbon dioxide from the air and turns into calcium carbonate, the substance of chalk and limestone. Lac hardens in the third way. It melts when it is warmed, and it sets hard again as it cools.
examples: A freshly painted room smells for days, as the last of the solvent leaves.
Nail polish dries in minutes, because its solvent evaporates fast.
A lime-washed wall often leaves white powder on a sleeve, because lime wash holds its pigment only weakly.
explanations.art: Three small panels: water rising as vapour from a painted wall, oxygen pairs arriving at a layer of oil paint, and a melted red stick cooling on a wooden toy.

explanations.definition: A by-product is a substance made along with the product. Pollution is a substance in the air, water or soil in an amount that harms living beings.
explanations.description: No factory makes only what it wants. Atoms cannot vanish, so every atom that goes in must come out somewhere. A good factory finds a use for its by-products. A urea factory makes carbon dioxide when it makes hydrogen. It then uses that carbon dioxide to make the urea. Other by-products are harder to use. Smoke, waste water and unwanted solids can harm people, other animals and plants. Products can harm too, after they leave the factory. Nitrogen fertiliser that the crop does not take up washes into ponds. There it feeds algae. When the algae die, the microbes who rot them use up the oxygen in the water, and fish die. Lead compounds were once common in paint. Lead damages the growing brain of a child, and no safe amount is known. Since 2017, house paint sold in India may hold only a trace of lead. A factory can also fail. In December 1984 a poisonous gas leaked from a pesticide factory in Bhopal, and thousands of people died. Chemists today try to design reactions that use less energy, make less waste and need no dangerous substances. This work is called green chemistry.
examples: A sugar mill burns its crushed cane as fuel and sells its molasses to make ethanol.
A pond below a heavily fertilised field turns green with algae.
Old paint that is flaking off a wall may hold lead, so it should not be scraped by children.
explanations.art: A factory with three outlets drawn in different colours: a truck of sacks, a pipe of by-product going back into the factory, and a chimney with a filter on it.

explanations.concept: Could the world be fed without factory fertiliser?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that factory nitrogen has greatly raised harvests. They disagree about how far farming could do without it.
explanations.description: Before 1913, all the nitrogen in crops came from dung, compost, bean crops, lightning and a little mined salt. The world then held about 1.8 billion people. Today it holds more than 8 billion. Factory fertiliser is one reason that so many can be fed. It also pollutes water, and making it burns a great deal of natural gas.
examples: A paddy field that gets nitrogen fertiliser usually gives much more grain than a field that gets none.
Sikkim has farmed without factory fertiliser since 2016.

perspectives.who: Scientists who count nitrogen, such as Vaclav Smil, and Jan Willem Erisman and his team in 2008
perspectives.explanation: About half of the nitrogen in the world's food now comes from factories. Without it, today's farmland could feed only about half of the people alive. Farming without it would need far more land, and forests would have to be cleared.

perspectives.who: Farmers and scientists who work on organic and natural farming
perspectives.explanation: Much factory nitrogen is wasted, because crops often take up less than half of what is spread. Bean crops, compost and careful use can replace a large part of it. Wasting less food would lower the need further.

explanations.art: A balance with a sack of fertiliser on one pan and a heap of compost and a bean plant on the other, with a crowd of people behind.

agreed.text: Substances made by living bodies can also be made in a laboratory from non-living materials.
agreed.evidence: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler heated a mineral salt called ammonium cyanate and got urea. It was the same as the urea in urine.

agreed.text: Nitrogen from the air can be made into fertiliser, and about half the world's food is now grown with it.
agreed.evidence: Fritz Haber made ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen in 1909, and Carl Bosch's factory opened in 1913. In 2008 Jan Willem Erisman's team estimated that this nitrogen feeds about 48 people in every 100.

agreed.text: Burning hydrocarbon fuels adds carbon dioxide to the air, and carbon dioxide holds heat.
agreed.evidence: Eunice Foote showed in 1856 that a tube of carbon dioxide warms more in sunlight than a tube of air. The share of carbon dioxide in the air has risen by about half since factories began.

agreed.text: A substance that helps at one dose can harm at a larger dose.
agreed.evidence: Every medicine label gives a largest safe dose. Hospitals treat people each year who took too much of a useful medicine, such as paracetamol or iron tablets.

agreed.text: A pigment needs a binder to stay on a surface.
agreed.evidence: In Three Paints, colour powder mixed with water alone rubs off when dry. Tests on old wall paintings, such as those at Ajanta, find glue mixed with the pigments.

agreed.text: Lead in paint harms children, and no safe amount of lead has been found.
agreed.evidence: In 1979 Herbert Needleman's team measured lead in children's milk teeth. Children with more lead did less well in class. The World Health Organization says no level of lead is known to be safe.

challenging.claim: Natural substances are safe, and substances made in a factory are harmful.
challenging.who: A common belief, and many advertisements.
challenging.for: Some factory products have done great harm, and many plant remedies have been used for centuries.
challenging.against: A molecule is the same wherever it was made. Urea from a factory and urea from urine cannot be told apart. Snake venom and some wild mushrooms are natural and deadly.

challenging.claim: The dose alone makes the poison.
challenging.who: Paracelsus, a Swiss doctor, in 1538, and most scientists since.
challenging.for: Salt, water, iron and every medicine help at one amount and harm at a larger one.
challenging.against: The rule needs care. For lead, no safe amount has been found. The same dose also acts differently on a baby, a child and a grown-up.

challenging.claim: More fertiliser always gives a bigger harvest.
challenging.for: A field with no fertiliser often gives a small crop, and the first bag raises the crop a lot.
challenging.against: A crop can take up only so much. Extra fertiliser is washed away or lost to the air. Much too much draws water out of the roots and harms the plant.

challenging.claim: Farming with compost and bean crops alone could feed everyone.
challenging.who: Many organic farmers and some farm scientists.
challenging.for: Much factory nitrogen is wasted today. Bean crops and compost can supply nitrogen without burning natural gas.
challenging.against: Scientists who count nitrogen estimate that factory nitrogen grows about half the world's food. Replacing all of it would need much more farmland.

challenging.claim: Hydrogen is a fuel with no pollution.
challenging.for: Hydrogen burns to give only water, with no carbon dioxide.
challenging.against: Most hydrogen today is made from natural gas, and that step gives off carbon dioxide. Hydrogen is clean only if it is made with clean energy.

challenging.for: Hoffmann's laboratory notes of August 1897 record that he made the substance.
challenging.against: Arthur Eichengrün, his senior at Bayer, later wrote that the work was done under his direction. Eichengrün was Jewish, and his name was left out during Nazi rule. In 2000 the historian Walter Sneader judged his claim likely to be true.

big_questions.q: Your body needs salt, and too much salt can make you ill. So is salt a food or a poison?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changed between the helpful salt and the harmful salt. Was it the salt?

big_questions.q: Urea from a factory and urea from your own body are the same substance. Does it matter where a substance was made?
big_questions.hint: Could any test tell the two apart? If none can, what is the difference?

big_questions.q: Some of the nitrogen in your muscles passed through a fertiliser factory. Is that part of you natural or made?
big_questions.hint: The nitrogen atom is the same atom it was in the air. Only its partners changed.

big_questions.q: Ammonia from Haber's reaction grows food for billions. It was also used to make explosives in a war. Is a discovery good or bad?
big_questions.hint: Think about a kitchen knife. Who decides what a knife does?

big_questions.q: A factory gives a town jobs and medicines. The people who live beside it breathe its smoke. Who should decide where a factory is built?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gains, who bears the harm, and whether they are the same people.

big_questions.q: Crude oil took millions of years to form. People may burn most of it within a few hundred years. What do we owe the people who come after us?
big_questions.hint: Think about the oil itself, and also about the carbon dioxide that burning it leaves in the air.

story.title: The Top That Left Its Colour Behind
story.note: Bhagya, Kiran and Ajji are made up. These facts are real: Channapatna in Karnataka is known for wooden toys turned on a lathe. Many are made of a pale wood called hale mara, or ivory wood. The colour is carried in lac, a resin made by lac insects. The lac is softened over heat and mixed with colour. A stick of it is pressed against the spinning wood. The heat of rubbing melts the lac. The toy is polished with a dry leaf of talegiri, the screw pine. Families in Karnataka set out steps of dolls at Dasara.
text: Bhagya had made the top herself, and by evening it had to be red.

She lived in Channapatna, on the road between Bengaluru and Mysuru, where half the street made toys. Her Ajji had turned wood on a lathe for forty years. That week Ajji had let Bhagya hold the chisel for the first time. Out of a block of pale hale wood had come a small top, a little lopsided, with a fat belly and a sharp foot.
Tomorrow was the first day of Dasara. Every house on the street would set out its steps of dolls. Bhagya wanted her top on the lowest step, shining red.
"Ajji, will you colour it?"
"After the order is done," said Ajji, without looking up. Sixty rattles were going to a shop in Mysuru, and forty-one of them were still bare wood.

Bhagya could not wait for forty-one rattles. She took a pinch of kumkum from the box beside the lamp and mixed it with water in a coconut shell. She painted the top with the frayed end of a twig. The red was so deep that she laughed aloud.
She set the top in the sun, and in a short while it was dry.
Her cousin Kiran came by with a string. "Let me spin it," he said. He was a year younger than Bhagya, and he could spin a top on his palm, which she could not.

He wound the string and threw. The top hummed across the cement floor. Where it had landed there was a small red ring, like a bangle drawn in chalk. When the top fell over, Kiran picked it up and looked at his fingers. They were red. So was the string.
The top was pink, with pale patches where his hand had been.
"Your colour is running away," he said.

"It is not thick enough. That is all." She mixed the kumkum again, as thick as dosa batter this time, and laid it on in a heavy coat. It took longer to dry. When it did, it cracked like the mud of a dry pond, and flakes fell off before anyone touched it.

She tried once more, with coconut oil in place of water. The colour went on smoothly and did not crack. It also did not dry. An hour later the top was still greasy, and it left a red print on the step where she put it down.
Bhagya sat in the doorway with the sticky top in her lap and watched her grandmother work. She had watched a thousand times. This time she watched the colour.

Ajji had no brush and no water. A rattle spun on the lathe so fast that its shape blurred. Ajji held a short red stick against it and pressed hard. The stick squealed, and a warm smell rose from it. Red flowed off the stick and around the wood in a band, as ghee spreads on a hot dosa. Then Ajji took the stick away and pressed a dry talegiri leaf against the spinning rattle. The red began to shine like a wet stone.
Ajji stopped the lathe and dropped the rattle into the basket. It landed on the others with a click. Nothing came off on anything.
"Ajji. Why does your red stay, and mine run away?"
Ajji looked at the top, and at Bhagya's red hands, and did not laugh. "What did you put on it?"
"Kumkum, with water. Then more kumkum. Then kumkum with oil."

"Kumkum is a powder," said Ajji. "Water carries a powder to the wood, and then the water goes away into the air. What is left? Powder, sitting on the wood as dust sits on a shelf. Nothing is holding it."
"And the oil?"
"Coconut oil holds it, but coconut oil never turns hard. You need something that carries the colour, and then turns hard and keeps it."
She opened a tin. Inside were lumps the colour of dark honey. "Lac. Tiny insects make it on the branches of trees in the forest. They cover themselves with it."
Ajji held a lump on an iron rod over the coals until it sagged like warm jaggery. Then she pushed the kumkum box towards Bhagya. "You mix. Fold it in."

Bhagya sprinkled the red powder on the soft lac and folded it over with a wooden stick, again and again. The powder disappeared into the lac. The lump turned red all the way through. Ajji rolled it on a stone into a stick as long as a finger and left it to cool. In a few minutes it was hard enough to tap on the floor.
"Now the colour is inside something," said Ajji. "Wash your top and bring it."

Bhagya scrubbed the top until it was pale wood again. Ajji fixed it on the lathe. She put the red stick in Bhagya's hand and closed her own hand over it. "Press. Harder. The rubbing makes the heat, and the heat melts the lac."
The stick squealed. Bhagya felt it soften against the wood, and she saw red run round the belly of her top. Ajji gave her the talegiri leaf, and the red began to shine.
When the top had cooled, Bhagya rubbed it hard on the inside of her wrist. Her wrist stayed brown.
Kiran wound the string and threw. The top hummed across the floor for a long time. Afterwards they both bent down to look. There was no ring on the cement.
"Is there lac on our front door too?" Kiran asked. "That is blue, and it does not come off."
Bhagya went to the door and scratched it with a fingernail. Then she looked at her nail, which was clean. "Something is holding it," she said. "I don't know what. But it will not be only colour."
story.epiphany: Bhagya's kumkum was only colour, so it rubbed off as soon as the water dried. Ajji folded the same kumkum into lac, which melts, carries the colour and sets hard. A colour stays on a surface only when a binder holds it there.
ask: The water carried the kumkum to the wood. Why did the kumkum not stay when the water dried?
Coconut oil held the colour, but the top stayed greasy. What must a binder do that coconut oil does not do?
Kiran asked about the blue front door. How could you find out what holds its colour?
