games.title: Where Did It Start? The raw material cards
games.context: This is a card game about where products come from. Each card is spoken by a substance. You say which raw material that substance started as.

setup.art: Twenty-two cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with four small tokens marked Air, Crude oil or natural gas, Rock or mineral, and Living being in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another player slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 22 product cards: a substance speaks on the front, its raw material and the reason are on the back

items.f: I am the nitrogen in a bag of urea.
items.b: Air. A factory joins nitrogen from the air with hydrogen to make ammonia, and then urea. Family: fertiliser.

items.f: I am the oxygen that a burning fuel joins with.
items.b: Air. About one fifth of the air is oxygen. Family: fuel.

items.f: I am the gas that turns lime wash hard on a wall.
items.b: Air. Carbon dioxide from the air turns lime into calcium carbonate. Family: paint.

items.f: I am the gas that makes oil paint go hard.
items.b: Air. Oxygen reacts with the oil and links its molecules together. Family: paint.

items.f: I fill the oxygen cylinder beside a hospital bed.
items.b: Air. Air is cooled until it turns liquid, and the oxygen is separated. Family: medicine.

items.f: I am the cooking gas in an LPG cylinder.
items.b: Crude oil or natural gas. LPG is the part with the shortest carbon chains. Family: fuel.

items.f: I am the petrol in a scooter.
items.b: Crude oil or natural gas. A refinery separates petrol from crude oil by boiling. Family: fuel.

items.f: I am the wax of a candle.
items.b: Crude oil or natural gas. Candle wax has long chains of 20 to 40 carbon atoms. Family: fuel.

items.f: I am the hydrogen that joins nitrogen to make ammonia.
items.b: Crude oil or natural gas. Most hydrogen is made from natural gas and steam. Family: fertiliser.

items.f: I am the binder in most wall paint, a kind of plastic.
items.b: Crude oil or natural gas. The plastic binder is made from substances that a refinery supplies. Family: paint.

items.f: I am the paracetamol in a fever tablet.
items.b: Crude oil or natural gas. Paracetamol is made in a few reactions from phenol, which comes from crude oil. Family: medicine.

items.f: I am the white pigment in wall paint.
items.b: Rock or mineral. Titanium dioxide is made from a black sand mined on beaches in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Family: paint.

items.f: I am red ochre, the red of very old rock paintings.
items.b: Rock or mineral. Red ochre is a soft rock coloured by iron oxide. Family: paint.

items.f: I am the phosphorus in a fertiliser bag.
items.b: Rock or mineral. Phosphate rock is mined, for example at Jhamarkotra in Rajasthan. Family: fertiliser.

items.f: I am potash, the potassium fertiliser.
items.b: Rock or mineral. Potash is mined from the salts of ancient dried-up seas. Family: fertiliser.

items.f: I am the chalky part of an antacid tablet.
items.b: Rock or mineral. Calcium carbonate comes from limestone. Family: medicine.

items.f: I am quinine, an old medicine for malaria.
items.b: Living being. Quinine comes from the bark of the cinchona tree. Family: medicine.

items.f: I am penicillin, which kills many bacteria.
items.b: Living being. Penicillin was first found in a mould called Penicillium. Family: medicine.

items.f: I am artemisinin, a newer medicine for malaria.
items.b: Living being. Tu Youyou's team drew it out of the sweet wormwood plant in 1972. Family: medicine.

items.f: I am biogas, burning under a village stove.
items.b: Living being. Microbes make biogas from dung and food waste. Family: fuel.

items.f: I am the ethanol mixed into petrol in India.
items.b: Living being. Yeast makes ethanol from the sugar of sugarcane. Family: fuel.

items.f: I am lac, the shining coat on a wooden toy.
items.b: Living being. Tiny lac insects make this resin on the branches of trees. Family: paint.

printables.title: 4 raw material tokens: Air, Crude oil or natural gas, Rock or mineral, Living being. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one raw material token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the raw material on the back scores 1 point.
A player who also names the family scores 1 more point. The four families are fertiliser, fuel, medicine and paint.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the raw material and the family aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each one you got right.
After all 22 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 44 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 22 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of four tokens.
flow.say: Each card is spoken by a substance in a product. Your four tokens are the four kinds of raw material. You say where the substance started.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take four tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Did It Start. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first eleven cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card five.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a raw material token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide which raw material the card describes?
good: I asked whether it is a gas from the air, something from oil, a rock or something alive.
Fuels like LPG and petrol come from crude oil.
Many medicines were first found in plants or moulds.

flow.parent: For a stuck child, ask: was this once part of the air, the ground, an oil well or a living being? One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Where Did It Start you play the first eleven product cards.

flow.do: Play the last eleven cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Eleven more cards. This time, also name the family. Is it a fertiliser, a fuel, a medicine or a paint?
flow.kid: Play eleven more cards. Name the family for each one.
flow.context: In this step of Where Did It Start you play the last eleven cards and name each family.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 22 cards into four heaps by raw material.
flow.say: Sort the cards into four heaps, one for each raw material. Look at the crude oil heap. How many of the four families are in it?
flow.kid: Sort the cards by raw material. Which families are in the crude oil heap?

check.q: Which raw material gives things for all four families: fertiliser, fuel, medicine and paint?
check.why: Natural gas gives the hydrogen for fertiliser. Crude oil gives fuels, the binder in wall paint and the starting substance for paracetamol. If you chose rock, check the heap: rock gives no fuel in this game.

flow.context: This is the last step of Where Did It Start. You sort the product cards into heaps by raw material.

games.title: Feed the Field: how much fertiliser is enough?
games.context: This is a game about the right amount of fertiliser. You are a farmer for six seasons. Each bean of fertiliser raises your harvest, but extra beans wash into the pond that everyone shares.

setup.art: A sheet of paper for each player with a large square drawn on it and labelled My Field, a bowl in the middle labelled Pond, and a heap of beans.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a field for each player. Put a bowl in the middle as the pond. Put 40 beans in a heap.

setup.art: A child placing two beans inside the square on her sheet while hiding it behind her other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Each season, secretly put 0, 1, 2 or 3 beans of fertiliser on your field.

setup.art: A die showing five, one bean being moved from each field into the bowl, and a score sheet with numbers.
setup.caption: 3. Roll the die for rain. Then count your harvest from the table.

printables.title: The harvest table: copy these seven lines on a sheet that everyone can see
items: The die shows 5 or 6: heavy rain. One bean from every field washes into the pond before the harvest.
0 beans left on the field: you harvest 2 bags of grain.
1 bean left on the field: you harvest 4 bags.
2 beans left on the field: you harvest 6 bags.
3 beans left on the field: you harvest 6 bags. The crop cannot use the third bean, so that bean goes into the pond.
Each bean you bought this season costs you 1 bag.
The pond holds 4 beans or more at the end of a season: algae cover the pond. Every player loses 3 bags. Then empty the pond.

printables.title: Score sheet: one row for each season, to write the beans bought, the rain, the bags harvested and the bags kept
items: Bags kept after paying for beans

rules: You need a die, about 40 beans, a bowl for the pond, and paper and a pencil. If you have no die, write 1 to 6 on six paper slips and draw one from a tumbler.
The game lasts six seasons. In each season, every player secretly puts 0, 1, 2 or 3 beans on their field. Then everyone shows their field.
One player rolls the die for everyone. On 1, 2, 3 or 4 the rain is light. On 5 or 6 the rain is heavy, and one bean from every field washes into the pond.
Count your harvest from the harvest table. Then take away 1 bag for each bean you bought, even a bean that washed away.
A third bean left on a field goes into the pond after the harvest. Used beans go back to the heap.
If the pond holds 4 beans or more at the end of a season, every player loses 3 bags. Then empty the pond.
A field that gets 0 beans for two seasons running gives only 1 bag the second time. The harvest took nutrients away, and nothing put them back.
After six seasons the player with the most bags wins. Playing alone? Play six seasons and try to keep more than 18 bags.

flow.do: Draw a field for each player. Copy the harvest table where all can see it. Put the bowl in the middle and the beans in a heap.
flow.say: You are a farmer. Each bean is one bag of fertiliser. Read the harvest table. How many beans do you think are best to use each season? Why?
flow.kid: Draw your field. Read the harvest table. How many beans will you use? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Feed the Field. You set up the fields, the pond and the harvest table.

flow.do: Play six seasons by the rules. After each season, every player writes one row on the score sheet.
flow.say: Put your beans down secretly. Now show them. I will roll for rain. Count your harvest, and pay one bag for each bean you bought.
flow.kid: Put down your beans. Roll for rain. Count your bags. Pay for your beans.

ask.q: Why does a third bean not give a bigger harvest?
good: The crop can only take up so much.
The extra is washed away.
More is not always better.

flow.parent: Two beans a season usually gives the most bags. Three beans is safe against heavy rain but always sends one bean to the pond. Let your child find this by playing.
flow.context: In this step of Feed the Field you play six seasons and write down each harvest.

flow.do: Add up the bags. Count how many beans went into the pond in the whole game. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: Add up your bags. How many beans went into the pond? Whose beans were they? Who lost bags when the algae came?
flow.kid: Add up your bags. Who put beans in the pond? Who paid for the algae?

check.q: In Feed the Field, why does a farmer who used 2 beans still lose bags when algae cover the pond?
options: 2 beans is too many for a field
check.why: The pond belongs to everyone, so harm from one field's extra fertiliser reaches all. If you chose 2 beans, check the table: the crop uses both. A real pond below many fields works the same way.

flow.context: This is the last step of Feed the Field. You count the bags and the beans that washed into the shared pond.

experiments.title: Three Paints: what keeps the colour on the card?
experiments.question: A colour powder mixed with water makes something that looks like paint. Does the colour stay on when it dries? Does rice paste or white glue in the mix change that?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When the three paints are dry, which will lose the most colour when you rub it? Which will lose the most when you wipe it with a damp cloth? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same colour powder, 1 level teaspoon, in every paint. Paint all the stripes on one card, the same size, and dry them together for the same time. Rub each stripe 10 times with a clean, dry fingertip, pressing equally hard. Wipe each stripe 5 times with a clean part of the damp cloth. Only one thing changes: what is mixed with the powder.
results_table: Dry rub: colour on the finger (0 none, 1 a little, 2 a lot)
Damp wipe: colour on the cloth (0 none, 1 a little, 2 a lot)

materials.item: colour powder, 3 level teaspoons: coloured kolam powder, kumkum, or 2 sticks of coloured chalk crushed fine
white craft glue, half a teaspoon (or liquid office gum)
soft cooked rice, 1 tablespoon, mashed smooth with 1 teaspoon of water
small bowls or katoris, each with its own teaspoon
a piece of stiff brown card, such as the side of a carton, about as big as a notebook page
paint brushes or cotton buds, one for each paint
a pencil, a ruler, a damp cotton cloth and a notebook

experiments.safety: Do not taste the paints. Crush chalk gently so that the dust does not fly, and wash your hands afterwards. Cover the table with newspaper.
experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows, for paint A, paint B and paint C. Write the dry rub score and the damp wipe score for each paint.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make three paints from the same colour powder. One has only water, one has rice paste and one has white glue. When they are dry, you rub and wipe them to see which keeps its colour.

setup.art: Three small steel bowls labelled A, B and C, each holding the same red powder, with a spoon of water, a spoon of white rice paste and a spoon of white glue beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put 1 teaspoon of powder and 1 teaspoon of water in each bowl. Add rice paste to B and glue to C.

setup.art: A brown card ruled into three rows labelled A, B and C, with two red stripes painted in each row.
setup.caption: 2. Paint two stripes of each paint on the card. Dry them under a fan for 30 minutes.

setup.art: A child's fingertip rubbing one dry red stripe, with red dust on the finger.
setup.caption: 3. Rub the first stripe of each paint 10 times with a dry finger. Look at your finger.

setup.art: A child's hand wiping the second stripe in a row with a damp white cloth, which has a red smear on it.
setup.caption: 4. Wipe the second stripe of each paint 5 times with a damp cloth. Look at the cloth.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: B: powder, water and rice paste
C: powder, water and white glue

flow.do: Show your child the colour powder, the rice paste and the white glue. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will make three paints from the same colour powder. Paint A has only water. Paint B has rice paste, and paint C has white glue. When they are dry, we will rub them. Which paint will lose the most colour? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three paints, one colour powder. Which paint will rub off most? Why?

ask.q: What do you think the rice paste or the glue might do to the powder?
good: It might stick the powder to the card.
It might hold the grains together.
It might do nothing, because the colour is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect all three to stay on, because all three look like paint when wet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Paints. You guess which of three home-made paints will keep its colour, before you test.

flow.do: Put 1 level teaspoon of colour powder in each of three bowls. Add 1 teaspoon of water to each. Add 1 teaspoon of rice paste to bowl B. Add half a teaspoon of white glue to bowl C. Stir each bowl with its own spoon until smooth.
flow.say: Every bowl gets the same powder and the same water. Bowl B also gets rice paste. Bowl C also gets glue. Why must the powder be the same in all three?
flow.kid: Put one teaspoon of powder in each bowl. Add water to all. Add rice paste to B. Add glue to C. Stir.
flow.parent: To make rice paste, mash 1 tablespoon of soft cooked rice with 1 teaspoon of water. Press with the back of a spoon until no grains show. Turmeric will not do as the powder, because it stains the card. If paint B is too thick to brush, add a few drops of water.
flow.context: In this step of Three Paints you mix one colour powder with water, with rice paste and with white glue.

flow.do: Rule the card into three rows and label them A, B and C. Paint two stripes in each row. Make each stripe as long as a finger and two fingers wide. Use a different brush for each paint.
flow.say: Paint two stripes of each paint. One stripe is for the dry rub, and one is for the damp wipe. Keep the coats thin and even.
flow.kid: Rule three rows: A, B and C. Paint two stripes in each row.
flow.context: In this step of Three Paints you paint two stripes of each paint on a brown card.

flow.do: Lay the card flat under a fan. Wait 30 minutes. A stripe is dry when it no longer feels cool to a light touch at its edge.
flow.say: Now the water must leave. Where is the water going? We will come back in half an hour.
flow.kid: Put the card under a fan. Wait 30 minutes.
flow.wait: Leave the card under a fan for 30 minutes
flow.parent: Use the wait for the story or the flashcards. On a damp day, or if paint B is thick, the stripes may need an hour.
flow.context: In this step of Three Paints you leave the painted card under a fan until all six stripes are dry.

flow.do: Your child rubs the first stripe of paint A 10 times with a clean, dry fingertip. They look at the finger and give a score of 0, 1 or 2. They repeat with B and C, using a clean finger each time. Then they wipe the second stripe of each paint 5 times with a clean part of a damp cloth. They score the cloth.
flow.say: Rub ten times, and press the same each time. Look at your finger. Is there no colour, a little or a lot? Now use a clean finger for the next paint.
flow.kid: Rub each first stripe 10 times. Score your finger. Wipe each second stripe 5 times. Score the cloth.

check.q: In Three Paints, why do you use a clean finger for each stripe?
options: So old colour is not counted twice
check.why: Colour left on the finger from paint A would look like colour from paint B. If you chose cool or faster, remember that a fair test changes only one thing at a time.

flow.parent: Score 0 for no colour, 1 for a faint mark and 2 for a clear patch of colour. Write each score down at once.
flow.context: In this step of Three Paints you rub each dry stripe with a finger. Then you wipe each with a damp cloth.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your six scores. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. All three paints had the same powder. What was different about the one that stayed?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Paint A had colour, and it spread like paint. What was missing from it?
good: Something to stick the powder to the card.
A glue or a binder.
The water left, and nothing held the powder.

ask.q: Paint B stayed on in the dry rub but smeared when wet. What does that tell you about rice paste?
good: Rice paste holds the powder when dry.
Water softens rice paste again.
It would not do for a wall in the rain.

flow.parent: In most homes paint A rubs off as dust. Paint B holds when dry but smears when wet, and paint C holds best. Write down what you really found, even if it differs. The reason: a colour powder is a pigment, and a pigment is only dust. Water spreads it and then evaporates. Paint needs a binder, a substance that dries into a solid and holds the pigment to the surface. Rice paste is a binder made of starch, but water softens starch again. White glue is a kind of plastic that holds better. Even white glue may smear a little. Wall paint for outdoors uses a binder that water cannot dissolve once it is dry.
flow.think: A lime-washed wall leaves white powder on your sleeve, and a painted door does not. What might be different in the two coats?
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Paints. You say what your scores show about powder, rice paste and glue.

experiments.title: One Dose, Two Bodies: why is a child's dose smaller?
experiments.question: A small glass of water and a big pot of water each get the same 2 drops of colour. Do they end up looking the same? How many drops does the pot need to match the glass?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. The pot holds ten times as much water as the glass. Will 2 drops colour both the same? How many drops will the pot need in all to match the glass? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both bodies hold the same tap water. Every drop comes from the same dropper, held the same way. Always compare in two clear glasses of the same size, filled to the same height, over white paper. A deep layer of coloured water looks darker than a shallow one, so the heights must match. Stir before you compare. Only one thing changes: the amount of water that the drops are spread through.
results_table: Drops in the pot so far
The pot water beside the small glass: paler, the same or darker?

materials.item: clear glasses or clear plastic tumblers of the same size
a pot or a jug that holds more than 1 litre
water: 100 millilitres for the glass (half a steel tumbler) and 1 litre for the pot (5 steel tumblers)
liquid food colour with a dropper top, or ink (or strong coffee, as the note in the second step says)
a drinking straw to use as a dropper, if the colour has no dropper top
a spoon for stirring, a sheet of white paper and a notebook

experiments.safety: Do not drink the coloured water. Food colour and ink stain clothes, so cover the table with newspaper. This is a model with colour. Never test with real medicine.
experiments.record: Write the number of drops in the pot each time you compare. Beside each number write paler, the same or darker.
experiments.context: In this experiment a small glass of water stands for a child's body. A big pot stands for a grown-up's body. You give both the same drops of colour, and find how many drops the pot needs to match the glass.

setup.art: A clear glass half full of water labelled small body, beside a large steel pot of water labelled big body, with a small bottle of blue food colour between them.
setup.caption: 1. Put 100 millilitres of water in a glass and 1 litre in a pot.

setup.art: A child squeezing two drops of blue colour into the glass, and two blue drops falling into the pot.
setup.caption: 2. Put 2 drops of colour in the glass and 2 drops in the pot. Stir both.

setup.art: Two clear glasses side by side on white paper, filled to the same height, one clearly blue and one almost clear.
setup.caption: 3. Fill a second glass from the pot to the same height. Compare the two over white paper.

setup.art: A child adding drops to the pot while a grown-up writes numbers in a notebook, with the two glasses on white paper nearby.
setup.caption: 4. Add drops to the pot, 2 at a time, until its water matches the small glass.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Drops in the pot so far
Pot water beside the small glass

flow.do: Pour 100 millilitres of water into one glass. Pour 1 litre into the pot. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: The glass is a small body, like a child's. The pot is a big body, like a grown-up's. The pot holds ten times as much water. Each will get 2 drops of colour. Will they look the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The glass is a small body. The pot is a big body. Each gets 2 drops. Will they match? Why?

ask.q: How many drops do you think the pot will need to look like the glass?
good: Ten times as many, so 20.
More than 2, because there is more water.
Any number with a reason.

flow.parent: Half a 200 millilitre steel tumbler is 100 millilitres. Five full tumblers make 1 litre. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Dose, Two Bodies. You set up a small glass and a big pot of water. You guess what 2 drops of colour will do to each.

flow.do: Put 2 drops of colour in the glass and 2 drops in the pot. Stir both. Fill the second glass from the pot to the same height as the first. Stand the two glasses on white paper.
flow.say: Both bodies have had the same dose, 2 drops. Look at the two glasses from the side. What do you see? Where did the colour in the pot go?
flow.kid: Put 2 drops in each. Stir. Fill the second glass from the pot. Compare them.
flow.parent: To drop from a straw, dip it in the colour and close the top with a finger. Lift it, then ease the finger to let one drop fall. Let your child practise over a plate first. If you have no food colour or ink, dissolve 3 teaspoons of instant coffee in 6 teaspoons of water. Then use a quarter teaspoon of this coffee wherever a step says 2 drops.
flow.context: In this step of One Dose, Two Bodies you give a glass and a pot the same 2 drops.

flow.do: Pour the sample back into the pot. Add 2 more drops to the pot and stir. Fill the second glass from the pot again and compare. Write paler, the same or darker. Repeat until the pot water matches the small glass.
flow.say: Pour the sample back. Add two more drops to the pot and stir. Fill the glass again to the same height. Is the pot water paler, the same or darker?
flow.kid: Add 2 drops to the pot. Stir. Fill the glass and compare. Write what you see.

check.q: In One Dose, Two Bodies, why must both glasses be filled to the same height?
options: A deeper layer of colour looks darker
The drops sink to the bottom
check.why: You look through the water, and more coloured water in the way looks darker. If you chose heavier or sinking, pour a little out of one glass and look again from above.

flow.parent: To save time, your child may add 4 drops at a time until the colours are close. Most families find a match between 18 and 22 drops.
flow.context: In this step of One Dose, Two Bodies you add drops to the pot until its water matches the glass.

flow.do: Empty the second glass and put 100 millilitres of fresh water in it. Add the pot's full number of drops to this glass. Stand it beside the first small glass.
flow.say: This new glass is another small body. We will give it the big body's dose. How does it look beside the first glass?
flow.kid: Fill the second glass with fresh water. Add the pot's number of drops. Compare.
flow.context: In this step of One Dose, Two Bodies you give a small glass the full dose that the pot needed.

flow.do: Look at the notes together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. The drops were the same each time. What made them look weak in the pot and strong in the glass?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The pot needed about ten times as many drops as the glass. Why ten?
good: The pot has ten times as much water.
The same drops are spread through more water.
To be equally strong, the dose must grow with the body.

ask.q: What does the last glass tell you about a child taking a grown-up's dose?
good: It would be far too strong for a small body.
The same amount is too much when the body is smaller.

flow.parent: The reason: the colour spreads evenly through all the water. Ten times the water makes each drop ten times weaker. A medicine spreads through the blood and the water of a body in a similar way. So a bigger body needs a bigger dose for the same effect. A grown-up's dose is too strong for a child. A real body is more than a pot of water. The liver and kidneys of a child also handle medicines differently. So a child's dose is never guessed. It comes from the label or a doctor.
flow.think: A farmer waters one pot plant and a whole field. What should she think about before she adds plant food to each?
flow.context: This is the last step of One Dose, Two Bodies. You say what the glass and the pot show about dose and body size.

activities.title: The Four Finds: a fuel, a medicine, a paint and a plant food at home

materials.item: your home, and a grown-up to walk round it with you
a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Find one fuel, one medicine, one paint and one plant food at home, and guess what each was made from.

activities.safety: A grown-up holds the medicine and keeps it closed. Look at the gas cylinder and the stove without touching the knobs. Do not open or smell paint, nail polish or fertiliser.
activities.record: Write four lines, one for each find: what it is, what it is for, and what you guess it was made from.
activities.context: In this activity you find one fuel, one medicine, one paint and one plant food in your own home. You guess what each was made from, before the unit tells you.

setup.art: A child and her mother looking at a red LPG cylinder under a kitchen counter, without touching it.
setup.caption: 1. Find a fuel, such as the LPG cylinder, a candle or a matchbox.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a strip of tablets and a tin of paint for a child to look at, with a pot plant and a small packet of plant food on a shelf behind.
setup.caption: 2. Find a medicine, a paint and a plant food. A grown-up holds them.

setup.art: A notebook page with four lines of writing, each ending in a question mark.
setup.caption: 3. For each find, write what you think it was made from.

flow.do: Walk round your home with your child. Find one fuel, one medicine, one paint and one plant food. Hold the medicine yourself. If you have no plant food, look at a pot plant and the soil in the pot.
flow.say: We are looking for four things. A fuel is something we burn for heat. A medicine treats an illness. A paint colours a surface. A plant food feeds a plant. What can you find?
flow.kid: Find a fuel, a medicine, a paint and a plant food. A grown-up holds the medicine.
flow.parent: A fuel could be the LPG cylinder, a candle or the petrol in a scooter. A paint could be a wall, a painted toy, nail polish or a child's paint box. A plant food could be a packet of fertiliser or compost.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Four Finds. You look for a fuel, a medicine, a paint and a plant food in your home.

flow.do: For each find, ask the two questions below. Write down every guess without correcting it.
flow.say: Look at each one. What do you notice? What do you think it was made from? Was it dug up, picked from a plant or made in a factory?
flow.kid: Look at each find. What do you notice? What was it made from? Write your guess.

ask.q: Do you think these four things have anything in common?
good: They were all made by people.
They all come from factories.
I am not sure yet.

flow.context: In this step of the Four Finds you guess what each of your four finds was made from.

flow.do: Ask your child what they wonder about the four finds. Write down one question for each. Then read the answers in the note below.
flow.say: What do you wonder about each one? Let us write one question for each. Now I will read what each was made from.
flow.kid: Write one question about each find. Then listen to what each was made from.
flow.parent: The answers: LPG and candle wax are separated from crude oil. Most paracetamol is made from a substance that comes from crude oil. The white in wall paint comes from a black beach sand. Its binder is a plastic made from crude oil. The nitrogen in fertiliser comes from the air. None of the four is found ready-made. Each is made by chemical reactions from a raw material.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Four Finds. You hear what your fuel, medicine, paint and plant food were made from.

activities.title: The Crude Oil Ladder: from cooking gas to candle wax

materials.item: a candle
a small tub of petroleum jelly
a plastic bag or a plastic bottle
a sheet of newspaper, a ruler and scissors
plates or bowls
the LPG stove or cylinder, to look at only

schedule.what: Feel four things made from crude oil, model their molecules with paper strips, and put them in order.

activities.safety: Look at the LPG stove and cylinder without turning any knob. Do not light the candle. A grown-up helps with the scissors if needed.
activities.record: Draw a ladder with five rungs. Write LPG, petrol, diesel, candle wax and plastic on the rungs, from the shortest chain to the longest.
activities.context: In this activity you collect things made from crude oil and model their molecules with paper strips. It shows why cooking gas, petrol and candle wax are so different, though all three come from one raw material.

setup.art: A candle, a tub of petroleum jelly and a plastic bag on a table, with an LPG stove in the background.
setup.caption: 1. Collect a candle, petroleum jelly and a plastic bag. Look at the LPG stove.

setup.art: Four plates holding paper strips of four lengths: very short, short, medium and long, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Cut five paper strips each of 3, 8, 16 and 30 centimetres. Put each length on its own plate.

setup.art: A child tipping a plate of short paper strips, which slide off easily, beside a plate of long strips tangled in a heap.
setup.caption: 3. Stir each plate with a finger, then tip it. Which strips slide and which tangle?

flow.do: Put the candle, the petroleum jelly and the plastic bag on a table. Look together at the LPG stove. Let your child feel the candle, the jelly and the bag.
flow.say: LPG is a gas. Petrol is a thin liquid. This jelly is soft, and this wax is hard. All of them were made from one thick, dark liquid called crude oil. How can one raw material give such different things? What do you think?
flow.kid: Feel the candle, the jelly and the bag. All came from crude oil. Why are they so different?

ask.q: What might be different inside a gas, a jelly and a hard wax?
good: The particles might be different sizes.
Some might hold together more strongly.
Any idea with a reason.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Crude Oil Ladder. You feel things made from crude oil and wonder why they differ.

flow.do: Cut newspaper strips about 1 centimetre wide. Cut five strips each of 3, 8, 16 and 30 centimetres. Put each length on its own plate. Your child stirs each plate with a finger and then tips it over a table.
flow.say: Each strip is a model of one molecule. One centimetre stands for one carbon atom. Stir each plate, then tip it. Which strips slide off freely? Which hold on to each other?
flow.kid: Cut strips of 3, 8, 16 and 30 centimetres. Stir each plate. Tip it. What happens?
flow.parent: The 3 centimetre strips stand for LPG and the 8 for petrol. The 16 stand for diesel and the 30 for candle wax. Short strips slide apart. Long strips lie across each other and move as a heap. Real long molecules also hold on to their neighbours at more places.
flow.context: In this step of the Crude Oil Ladder you cut paper strips of four lengths as models of hydrocarbon molecules.

flow.do: Tell your child which strip stands for which substance. Ask them to put the real things in order, from the shortest chain to the longest. Then ask where the plastic bag belongs.
flow.say: The 3 centimetre strips are LPG. The 8s are petrol, the 16s are diesel and the 30s are candle wax. Where would petroleum jelly go? A plastic molecule has thousands of carbon atoms. How long would its strip be?
flow.kid: Put LPG, petrol, diesel and wax in order. Where does the jelly go? Where does plastic go?

ask.q: A refinery separates crude oil by boiling. Which strips would boil away first?
good: The shortest ones, the LPG.
Short chains escape more easily.
Long chains hold on to each other, so they need more heat.

flow.parent: Petroleum jelly belongs between diesel and candle wax. A plastic chain of 10,000 carbon atoms would need a strip 100 metres long. That is why plastic is a tough solid.
flow.context: In this step of the Crude Oil Ladder you put five substances in order of chain length.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the ladder with five rungs. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Draw the ladder, with the shortest chain on the lowest rung. As the chains get longer, what happens to the substance?
flow.kid: Draw the ladder. What changes as the chains get longer?

check.q: What happens to hydrocarbons as their carbon chains get longer?
options: They get thicker and harder to boil
They get thinner and boil sooner
check.why: Longer chains hold on to their neighbours at more places. So the substance flows less and needs more heat to boil. If you chose thinner, look again at the long paper strips, which moved as one heap.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Crude Oil Ladder. You draw the ladder from LPG up to plastic.

activities.title: The Tea Factory: what goes in, and what comes out?

materials.item: water, 1 steel tumbler
tea leaves, 1 level teaspoon (or coffee powder for filter coffee)
milk and sugar, as your family likes
a small pot, a strainer, a teaspoon and the stove
a notebook page with two columns, headed IN and OUT

schedule.what: Make one tumbler of tea with a grown-up and list everything that goes in and everything that comes out.

activities.safety: A grown-up lights the stove, boils the tea and pours it. The child stands back from the steam and writes the lists.
activities.record: Fill the two columns, IN and OUT. Beside each thing in the OUT column write product, by-product or waste.
activities.context: In this activity you make one tumbler of tea and list everything that goes in and everything that comes out. A kitchen making tea works as a small factory does, with raw materials, a product, by-products and waste.

setup.art: A tumbler of water, a teaspoon of tea leaves, a little milk and sugar laid out beside a stove, and a notebook with two columns headed IN and OUT.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out everything that will go in. Write each one in the IN column.

setup.art: A grown-up boiling tea in a small pot on a gas stove, with steam rising, while a child writes in a notebook at a safe distance.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up makes the tea. Watch what leaves the pot.

setup.art: A strainer full of wet tea leaves over a tumbler of tea, with a notebook where each thing in the OUT column has a label beside it.
setup.caption: 3. List everything that came out. Label each one product, by-product or waste.

flow.do: Lay out the water, tea leaves, milk and sugar. Your child measures the tea leaves with a level teaspoon and writes everything in the IN column. Ask what else goes in that cannot be seen on the table.
flow.say: This kitchen is our factory, and tea is the product. Write down every raw material. What else will go in that is not on the table? What do you think will come out besides tea?
flow.kid: Write everything that goes in. What goes in that you cannot see? What will come out?

ask.q: What goes into making tea that is not on the table?
good: The gas for the flame.
Air, because the flame needs oxygen.
Heat.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Tea Factory. You list everything that goes into making one tumbler of tea.

flow.do: Make the tea as you usually do. Ask your child to watch for everything that leaves the pot. Strain the tea into the tumbler. When the used leaves have cooled, your child measures them with the teaspoon.
flow.say: Watch the pot. What is leaving it? What is the flame making? After I strain the tea, measure the used leaves with the teaspoon.
flow.kid: Watch what leaves the pot. Measure the used tea leaves when they are cool.
flow.parent: Steam leaves the pot. The flame makes carbon dioxide and water vapour, which cannot be seen, and heat. One teaspoon of dry leaves swells to about two or three teaspoons of wet leaves.
flow.context: In this step of the Tea Factory a grown-up makes the tea while you watch what comes out.

flow.do: Your child writes everything that came out in the OUT column. Together, label each one as product, by-product or waste.
flow.say: Tea is the product. What else came out? Which of those things could still be used? We call a useful one a by-product. What can nobody use?
flow.kid: List everything that came out. Label each one: product, by-product or waste.

ask.q: What could the used tea leaves be used for?
good: They can go into compost.
They can be mixed into the soil of a pot plant.
They need not go in the dustbin.

flow.parent: Out: tea, used leaves, steam, carbon dioxide, heat and the water used for washing up. Used leaves are a by-product if they go to compost. They are waste if they go to the dustbin.
flow.context: In this step of the Tea Factory you sort what came out into product, by-product and waste.

flow.do: Read your child the urea factory list in the note below. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Here is what goes into a urea factory, and what comes out. Listen for a by-product that the factory uses again. Which one is it?
flow.kid: Listen to the urea factory list. Which by-product does the factory use again?

check.q: A urea factory makes carbon dioxide as a by-product. What does it do with much of it?
options: Uses it to make the urea
check.why: Urea is made by joining ammonia with carbon dioxide, so the factory feeds its own by-product back in. If you chose cooking gas, remember that carbon dioxide does not burn.

flow.parent: A urea factory. In: air, natural gas, water and energy. Out: urea, carbon dioxide and heat. The carbon dioxide comes from making hydrogen, and the factory uses much of it to make the urea.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Tea Factory. You compare your tea lists with what goes into and comes out of a urea factory.

projects.title: The Fuel Diary: three days of everything your family burns

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
a clock or a phone timer
the family, to answer questions

projects.safety: A grown-up works the stove. The child only watches the clock and writes.

schedule.what: List every fuel your family uses in a day, and what each one is used for.
Time how many minutes the stove burns in one day.
Try one change that saves fuel, time the stove again and compare.

projects.record: Day 1: a list of fuels and their uses. Day 2: the minutes the stove burned, meal by meal. Day 3: the change you tried, the new minutes and the difference.
projects.context: In this three-day project you list every fuel your family burns and time how long the stove is lit. Then you try one change that saves fuel. It shows how much fuel one home uses, and where the carbon dioxide comes from.

setup.art: A notebook page with a list: LPG for cooking, petrol for the scooter, diesel for the school bus, and a plug for electricity, each with a small drawing.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: list every fuel your family uses, and what it does.

setup.art: A child with a notebook watching a wall clock while a grown-up cooks on a gas stove.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: write the time whenever the stove is lit and put out. Add up the minutes.

setup.art: A pot on a gas stove with its lid on, and a notebook showing two totals, one circled.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: try one change, such as a lid on every pot. Time the stove again.

flow.do: Day 1. Sit with your child and list every fuel the family used today. Include cooking, travel and electricity. Ask for a guess: which use burns the most fuel?
flow.say: Let us list everything we burned today. What cooked the food? What moved the bus or the scooter? Which do you think used the most fuel? Why?
flow.kid: List every fuel your family used today. Which used the most? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Most electricity in India is made by burning coal, so count the fan and the lights too. A walk or a cycle ride burns only food.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Fuel Diary. You list every fuel your family burns in one day.

flow.do: Day 2. Each time the stove is lit, your child writes the time. They write the time again when the flame is put out. In the evening, add up the minutes.
flow.say: Today you are the timekeeper. Write the time when I light the stove and when I put it out. Tonight we will add up the minutes.
flow.kid: Write the time when the stove is lit. Write when it goes out. Add the minutes.
flow.parent: If two burners are lit together, count the minutes of each. A family of four often totals between 60 and 120 burner minutes a day.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Fuel Diary. You time how many minutes the gas stove burns in one day.

flow.do: Day 3. Choose one change together and use it all day. Time the stove as on day 2. Compare the two totals.
flow.say: Choose one change. We could keep a lid on every pot, or soak the dal first, or use the pressure cooker. Time the stove again. Did the minutes go down? Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why.
flow.kid: Pick one change. Time the stove again. Did the minutes go down? Say why.

ask.q: Every minute of flame turns LPG into carbon dioxide. What does saving 10 minutes a day mean over a year?
good: 3,650 minutes less burning.
Less gas bought and less carbon dioxide made.
Small savings add up.

flow.parent: The meals differ from day to day, so a small difference may be chance. A difference of more than about 10 minutes is likely to be real. A lid keeps heat in the pot, so the food cooks sooner.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Fuel Diary. You try one change that saves fuel and compare the stove minutes with day 2.

challenges.title: The Slow Tablet: let the colour out late, but not too late
challenges.problem: Some medicines must not be let out all at once. A slow tablet lets its medicine out a little later, or a little at a time. Your problem is the same. Instant coffee powder is your pretend medicine, and it colours water within seconds. Build a tablet that keeps the water clear for 5 minutes. It must then turn the water brown before 15 minutes are up.
constraints: The medicine is a quarter teaspoon of instant coffee powder. This is a model, and nobody eats the tablet.
The finished tablet must be no bigger than a large marble, about 2 centimetres across.
Drop the tablet into a clear glass of water at room temperature. Do not stir, shake or touch it.
No brown may show in the water for the first 5 minutes.
Brown must show clearly before 15 minutes are up.
You may use only kitchen things, such as atta dough, ghee, oil, paper and sugar.
materials: instant coffee powder, about 2 teaspoons (or sugar wetted with a few drops of food colour)
atta mixed with a little water into a stiff dough, about as much as a lemon
a little ghee or cooking oil, a pinch of sugar and a strip of paper
3 clear glasses of water at room temperature
a clock or a phone timer, a sheet of white paper and a notebook
general: Wrap the coffee in a ball of atta dough and pinch the join shut.
Rub a thin coat of ghee over a dough ball, so that water gets in more slowly.
Change the thickness of the dough wall: thicker to slow the tablet, thinner to hurry it.
creative: Make a small hole in the dough wall and plug it with a sugar crystal. The hole opens when the sugar dissolves.
Knead the coffee into the dough itself, so that it comes out a little at a time. Real slow tablets often hold the medicine inside a solid in this way.
Make two layers with ghee between them. Some real tablets have a coat that the stomach's acid cannot open, so they open only in the intestine.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own slow tablet. It must pass both tests: clear water at 5 minutes, and brown water before 15 minutes. Draw your design, write the time when brown first showed, and write what you would change next.
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a pretend tablet from atta dough and coffee powder. It must keep its colour in for 5 minutes and let it out before 15 minutes. Medicine makers solve the same problem when a medicine must be let out late or slowly.

setup.art: A quarter teaspoon of brown coffee powder being wrapped inside a small flat disc of dough on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap a quarter teaspoon of coffee powder in dough. Keep it smaller than a large marble.

setup.art: A small dough ball at the bottom of a clear glass of water standing on white paper, with a clock beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Drop the tablet into a glass of water. Start the clock. Do not stir.

setup.art: The same glass with a brown cloud spreading from the dough ball, and a notebook with a time written in it.
setup.caption: 3. Write the time when brown first shows. Is it between 5 and 15 minutes?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Let your child drop a pinch of bare coffee powder into a glass of water and watch.
flow.say: First, drop in a pinch of coffee with no coat. How long does the colour take to show? Now think. What could keep the water away from the coffee for five minutes?
flow.kid: Drop a pinch of coffee in water. How fast does it colour? What could slow it?

ask.q: What must happen before the coffee can colour the water?
good: Water must reach the coffee.
The coffee must dissolve and spread.
So a coat must keep water out for a while.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Slow Tablet. You watch how fast bare coffee powder colours water.

flow.do: Your child chooses a design and builds one tablet. Check that it is no bigger than a large marble. Ask them to guess its time and give a reason.
flow.say: Build your first tablet. How thick will you make the wall? When do you think the brown will show? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Build your tablet. Keep it small. Guess when the brown will show. Why?
flow.parent: A first try is often a dough ball with a wall about as thick as a chapati. Let your child choose, even if you expect it to fail.
flow.context: In this step of the Slow Tablet you design and build your first tablet from dough and coffee powder.

flow.do: Stand a glass of water on white paper. Your child drops the tablet in and starts the clock. They look every minute and write the time when brown first shows. Stop at 15 minutes.
flow.say: Drop it in and start the clock. Look every minute, but do not touch the glass. Tell me the moment you see brown.
flow.kid: Drop the tablet in. Start the clock. Look every minute. Write when brown shows.
flow.parent: Times differ a lot. A thin or cracked wall may leak in under a minute. A thick ball may hold for over an hour. Use the waiting time to plan the next design.
flow.context: In this step of the Slow Tablet you test your tablet in water and time when the colour comes out.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Then they change one thing and plan a second tablet.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Was your tablet too fast, too slow or just right? Change one thing only. What will you change?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw and why. Change one thing. Plan the next tablet.

check.q: A slow tablet let its colour out after 1 minute. Which single change is most likely to slow it?
options: A thicker wall with the join pinched shut
check.why: Water must cross the wall to reach the coffee, so a thicker, well-closed wall takes longer. If you chose warmer water, remember that warmth speeds up dissolving. More coffee changes the colour, not the time.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Slow Tablet. You say what happened to your tablet and plan a better one.

worksheets.title: Where things come from, and what a paint needs

items.p: Where does the nitrogen in urea fertiliser come from?
items.why: About four fifths of the air is nitrogen gas. A factory joins it with hydrogen to make ammonia, and then urea.

items.p: Match each product to the raw material it starts from.
items.why: Each product is made from a raw material taken from nature. The four here come from under the ground, the air, a living tree and a rock.

items.p: The part of a paint that sticks the pigment to the wall is the ____.
items.why: The binder dries into a solid that holds the pigment and grips the surface.

items.p: A pigment mixed with water alone makes a paint that stays on.
items.why: False. When the water evaporates, only loose powder is left. A paint needs a binder to hold the pigment.

items.p: Sort these into four families: fertiliser, fuel, medicine or paint.
items.why: Fertilisers feed plants, fuels are burned for heat, medicines treat illness, and paints colour and protect surfaces.

items.p: What do the letters N, P and K on a fertiliser bag stand for?
items.why: N, P and K are the chemical symbols of the three main plant nutrients. K comes from kalium, an old name for potassium.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest carbon chain to the longest.
items.why: LPG has 3 or 4 carbon atoms in a chain, and petrol has about 5 to 12. Diesel has about 12 to 20, and candle wax about 20 to 40.

items.p: Burning a hydrocarbon fuel makes carbon dioxide and water.
items.why: True. The carbon atoms join with oxygen to make carbon dioxide, and the hydrogen atoms join with oxygen to make water.

items.p: Why is a child's dose of medicine smaller than a grown-up's?
items.why: A medicine spreads through the body. In a smaller body the same amount is stronger, so a child needs less.

items.p: A substance that a factory makes along with its product is called a ____.
items.why: A by-product is made at the same time as the product. Some by-products can be used, and some are waste.

items.p: In Three Paints, the powder mixed with only water rubbed off. Explain why in two sentences.
items.a: The water spread the powder on the card and then evaporated. Nothing was left to hold the powder, so it rubbed off as dust.
items.why: A strong answer says where the water went, and that the paint had no binder.

items.p: In One Dose, Two Bodies, 2 drops looked dark in the glass and pale in the pot. Explain why.
items.a: The pot held ten times as much water as the glass. The same drops were spread through more water, so each part of the water got less colour.
items.why: A strong answer says that the amount of colour was the same, and that the amount of water was different.

items.p: Draw a drop of wet paint, seen through a magnifying glass. Label the pigment, the binder and the solvent.
items.a: Small coloured grains labelled pigment. A sticky substance around the grains labelled binder. A liquid that carries both, labelled solvent, with an arrow showing it leaving into the air.
items.why: A strong drawing shows three separate parts. It shows that the solvent leaves, and that the binder and the pigment stay.
items.art: A large empty circle, as the view through a magnifying glass, above a strip of wall.

items.p: Should a farmer use factory fertiliser on a paddy field?

views.says: Urea gives me a bigger harvest from the same field. Without it I could not grow enough to sell.

views.who: A fisher who works on the pond below the field
views.says: Rain washes the extra urea into my pond. The water turns green, and my fish die.
Use it, but measure it. Give the crop what it can take up, while it is growing, and no more.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about fertiliser. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that a harvest carries nutrients away, so something must put them back. Another is that a crop cannot use extra fertiliser, and the extra feeds algae in ponds.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses a fact about fertiliser, such as what the crop takes up and where the rest goes.

items.p: Which raw material do most plastics and wall-paint binders start from?
items.why: A refinery supplies the starting substances for plastics. The binder in most wall paint is a plastic of this kind.

worksheets.title: Why each product works as it does

items.p: A refinery separates crude oil into its parts. What does it use to separate them?
items.why: Short carbon chains boil at low temperatures and long chains at high temperatures. So each part is collected at its own height in the tower.

items.p: Water-based wall paint dries on a wall. What happens to its water?
items.why: The water is the solvent. It evaporates, and the binder particles join into a sheet that holds the pigment.

items.p: Why does lime wash turn hard on a wall?
opts: It reacts with carbon dioxide from the air
items.why: Lime takes in carbon dioxide and becomes calcium carbonate, the substance of chalk and limestone. This is a chemical reaction.

items.p: A crop takes up half of the urea spread on a field. Where can the other half go?
opts: Into ponds, rivers and the air
items.why: Atoms cannot vanish. Nitrogen that the crop does not take up is washed away by rain or lost to the air as gases.

items.p: Carbon dioxide is harmful in any amount, however small.
items.why: False. You breathe it out, and plants need it. A little in the air keeps the Earth warm enough to live on. The harm comes from too much.

items.p: Burning 1 kilogram of LPG makes less than 1 kilogram of carbon dioxide.
items.why: False. It makes about 3 kilograms. The extra mass is oxygen from the air, which joins with the carbon of the fuel.

items.p: Sort these coats by how they turn hard.
cats: It reacts with a gas in the air
items: It reacts with a gas in the air
It reacts with a gas in the air
items.why: Wall paint and nail polish lose their solvent. Oil paint reacts with oxygen, and lime wash with carbon dioxide. Melted lac sets as it cools.

items.p: Three of these medicines were first found in a plant or a mould. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Quinine comes from cinchona bark, penicillin from a mould and artemisinin from sweet wormwood. Chalky antacid is made from limestone, a rock.

items.p: A made-up medicine needs 10 milligrams for each kilogram of body mass. How many milligrams suit a 25 kilogram child?
items.why: 10 milligrams for each of 25 kilograms is 10 times 25, which is 250 milligrams.

items.p: Put the steps of making and using urea in order.
items: Join ammonia with carbon dioxide to make urea
Spread the urea on the field
Join nitrogen with hydrogen to make ammonia
a: Join nitrogen with hydrogen to make ammonia
Join ammonia with carbon dioxide to make urea
Spread the urea on the field
items.why: Nitrogen gas is first made into ammonia. The ammonia is then made into urea, a solid that is easy to carry and spread.

items.p: Some people think three bags of fertiliser must grow three times the crop of one bag. Explain what really happens.
items.a: The first bag raises the harvest a lot. A crop can take up only so much, so the extra is washed into ponds or lost to the air. Much too much can draw water out of the roots and harm the plants.
items.why: A strong answer says that a crop has a limit, and says where the extra fertiliser goes.

items.p: Why does a flame need plenty of air to burn cleanly? Say what it makes with too little air.
items.a: Burning joins the fuel with oxygen from the air. With enough oxygen, a flame makes carbon dioxide and water. With too little, it also makes soot and a poisonous gas called carbon monoxide.
items.why: A strong answer names oxygen, and names soot or carbon monoxide as what a starved flame makes.

items.p: A plant medicine stopped working after the plant was boiled. Give one reason why heat might matter.
items.a: Heat can break the molecule that does the work, or change it into another substance. So a cold method of drawing it out may keep the medicine whole.
items.why: A strong answer says that the medicine is a particular molecule, and that heat can break or change a molecule.

items.p: Is a natural substance safer than one made in a factory?

views.says: I trust medicines and colours that come straight from plants. People have used them for hundreds of years.
A molecule is the same wherever it was made. Factory urea and the urea in urine cannot be told apart. Snake venom is natural and deadly.
What matters is the dose and the testing. A plant medicine can also harm if the amount is wrong.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about medicines and dose. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that long use gives some evidence of safety. Another is that the same molecule acts the same wherever it comes from. The amount decides whether it helps or harms.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer separates where a substance comes from, how much is taken and how well it was tested.

items.p: Label four outlets on this picture of a refinery tower: LPG, petrol, diesel and bitumen.
a: LPG: the outlet at the very top
Petrol: the outlet just below the top
Diesel: an outlet in the lower half
Bitumen: the outlet at the bottom
items.why: Short chains boil most easily and rise highest, so LPG leaves at the top. Bitumen has the longest chains and stays at the bottom.
items.art: A tall refinery tower with four pipes leaving it at different heights, each with a blank label line.

worksheets.title: Testing ideas about dose, waste and fuel

items.p: A new fuel burns to give only water. What must we still ask about it?
opts: How the fuel itself was made
items.why: Hydrogen burns to give only water. But most hydrogen is made from natural gas, and that step gives off carbon dioxide.

items.p: A paint stays on in a dry rub but smears when wet. What does this show about its binder?
items.why: The binder holds the pigment while dry, as rice paste does. Water softens it, so it would not last on an outside wall.

items.p: Which finding first showed that a substance from living bodies can be made from non-living materials?
opts: Urea made from a mineral salt
items.why: Urea is made by the body. In 1828 it was made in a laboratory from a mineral salt, with no kidney involved.

items.p: A factory doubles what it makes, and changes nothing else. What happens to its by-products?
items.why: Each batch of product comes with its by-products. Twice the product by the same reactions gives twice the by-products.

items.p: Scientists have found a small amount of lead that is safe for children.
items.why: False. Harm to the growing brain has been found at every amount measured. That is why lead is now kept out of house paint.

items.p: A medicine that kills germs in a glass dish is ready to be sold.
items.why: False. It must still be tested for years, first in the laboratory and then on thousands of volunteers. Most new medicines fail these tests.

items.p: Match each cause to its result.
pairs: Too much urea on a field
Too little air for a flame
A grown-up's dose in a child
items.why: In each pair an amount or a missing part explains the result. Extra nitrogen feeds algae, and a starved flame burns badly. Loose pigment falls off, and a small body makes a dose stronger.

items.p: Urea is 46 parts nitrogen in 100. To the nearest kilogram, how much nitrogen does a 45 kilogram bag hold?
items.why: 46 hundredths of 45 is 20.7 kilograms, which rounds to 21 kilograms. Nearly half of every bag was once nitrogen gas in the air.

items.p: Designing reactions that make less waste and need no dangerous substances is called ____ chemistry.
items.why: Green chemistry tries to prevent waste and harm in the design of a reaction, before a factory is built.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does paint keep a steel nail from rusting? Say what you would keep the same.
items.a: Take two nails of the same kind. Paint one all over and leave one bare. Keep both in the same damp place for the same number of days. Then compare the rust on each.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the paint. It keeps the nails, the place and the time the same.

items.p: Lead harms children at every amount measured. Does lead break the rule that only the dose decides? Explain.
items.a: Lead still follows part of the rule, because more lead does more harm. But the rule also suggests that a small enough amount is harmless. For lead no such amount has been found.
items.why: A strong answer sees both sides. More is worse, as the rule says, and yet no safe amount is known.

items.p: A town is offered a medicine factory that will bring jobs. Write two questions the town should ask first.
items.a: For example: What by-products and waste will the factory make, and where will they go? What happens if a gas or a liquid leaks, and who will warn the people living nearby?
items.why: Strong questions are about by-products, waste, safety or who bears the harm. They cannot be answered with yes or no.

items.p: A 60 kilogram grown-up takes a certain dose. Why is half not always right for a 30 kilogram child?
items.a: Body mass is only one thing that matters. A child's liver and kidneys handle some medicines differently, and some medicines are not for children at all. So the label or a doctor decides.
items.why: A strong answer says that halving the mass is a fair first thought. It then gives a reason why a real body is not a pot of water.

items.p: Should a city stop all petrol and diesel vehicles next year?

views.says: My bus runs on diesel and carries sixty people to work. Until electric buses and chargers reach my town, stopping would strand them.
Every litre burnt adds carbon dioxide that stays in the air for hundreds of years. The sooner we stop, the less the Earth warms.
We can change step by step. Cleaner fuels, electric vehicles and fewer wasted journeys each cut some, starting today.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about fuels. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that burning fuel always makes carbon dioxide, which holds heat. Another is that people need the energy for work and travel. So a change needs something to take the fuel's place.
items.why: This is a real trade-off with no single right answer. A strong answer uses a fact about burning, and answers another view fairly.

items.p: Draw a flow chart of a urea factory. Show what goes in, the product, and one by-product.
items.a: Arrows going in: air, natural gas, water and energy. An arrow going out to urea, the product. Another arrow going out to carbon dioxide, a by-product, with a loop taking it back in to make the urea.
items.why: A strong chart shows raw materials going in and more than one thing coming out. The best ones show the by-product being used again.
items.art: An empty box labelled Urea factory, with blank arrows on its left and right.

quiz.p: Fertilisers, medicines, fuels and paints are all made in which way?
opts: By chemical reactions from raw materials
quiz.why: Each is made by changing a raw material into a new substance. The raw material may be air, rock, crude oil or a plant.

quiz.p: Which of these is a raw material?
quiz.why: Crude oil is taken from nature as it is. Petrol, paracetamol and wall paint are all products made from raw materials.

quiz.p: Why do farmers add nitrogen fertiliser to a field?
quiz.why: The nitrogen inside a crop leaves the field with the harvest. Fertiliser puts nitrogen back for the next crop.

quiz.p: What can happen when too much fertiliser washes into a pond?
quiz.why: The extra nitrogen feeds algae. When the algae die and rot, the oxygen in the water is used up, and fish cannot breathe.

opts: A substance that gives heat on burning
A gas found only in air
quiz.why: A fuel stores energy and gives it out as heat when it burns. A fuel can be a gas, a liquid or a solid.

quiz.p: Which two substances does burning LPG mainly make?
quiz.why: LPG is made of carbon and hydrogen. Joined with oxygen, the carbon becomes carbon dioxide and the hydrogen becomes water.

quiz.p: Which of these medicines was first found in a mould?
quiz.why: Penicillin comes from the mould Penicillium. Quinine, aspirin and artemisinin each began with a plant.

quiz.p: Why are new medicines tested on many volunteers before they are sold?
opts: To check they work and are safe
quiz.why: A substance may work in a glass dish and still fail or harm in a body. Only careful tests on many people can show that.

quiz.p: The same dose goes into a small body and a big body. In which is it stronger?
opts: It has no strength in either
quiz.why: In a small body the dose is spread through less blood and water. This is what the dark small glass showed in One Dose, Two Bodies.

quiz.p: What does the solvent in a paint do?
opts: Makes the paint thin enough to spread
Sticks the pigment to the wall
quiz.why: The solvent carries the pigment and the binder, and then evaporates. The pigment gives colour and the binder does the sticking.

opts: A substance present in a harmful amount
quiz.why: A substance pollutes when there is enough of it, in the air, water or soil, to harm living beings. The amount matters.

quiz.p: Urea can be made only inside a living body.
quiz.why: False. In 1828 urea was made in a laboratory from a mineral salt. Today factories make it from air, natural gas and water.

applications: Farmers get a soil test before they buy fertiliser. The test shows which nutrient the field lacks, so that only that nutrient is added.
Urea sold in India is coated with neem oil. The coating slows the release of nitrogen, so more of it reaches the crop.
A medicine label gives the dose by age or by body mass. A syrup comes with a measuring cap so that the dose is exact.
Petrol in India has ethanol mixed into it. The ethanol is made from sugarcane and grain, so a little less crude oil is burned.
House paint sold in India since 2017 may hold only a trace of lead. Older paint that is flaking is removed with care for this reason.
Ships, bridges and bicycles are painted to keep air and water away from the steel. Then the steel does not rust.

open_questions.q: Can ammonia be made from air without high heat, high pressure and natural gas?
open_questions.why_open: Some bacteria make ammonia at the temperature of the soil, using an enzyme. Chemists have not yet matched this in a factory.

open_questions.q: Can a fuel be made in huge amounts that adds no carbon dioxide to the air?
open_questions.why_open: Hydrogen, biofuels and fuels made from captured carbon dioxide all work in small amounts. Each is still costly or needs a great deal of clean energy.

open_questions.q: Why does the same medicine work well in one person and poorly in another?
open_questions.why_open: Bodies differ in how fast they break a medicine down. Scientists can explain this for some medicines, but not yet for most.

open_questions.q: Where will new medicines against resistant bacteria come from?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria become resistant faster than new antibiotics are found. Scientists are searching in soil microbes, the deep sea and insects, with few successes so far.

open_questions.q: What happens to paint after it flakes off walls, ships and roads?
open_questions.why_open: Flakes of paint break into very small plastic particles. Nobody yet knows how much of this reaches the sea, or what it does to living beings there.

maths.problem: In One Dose, Two Bodies, a glass with 100 millilitres of water got 2 drops of colour. The pot holds 1 litre. How many drops does the pot need to be equally strong? How many would a bucket of 5 litres need?
maths.answer: The pot needs 20 drops. The bucket needs 100 drops.
maths.explain: 1 litre is 1,000 millilitres, which is 10 times 100 millilitres. So the pot needs 10 times 2 drops, which is 20. 5 litres is 50 times 100 millilitres, and 50 times 2 is 100.
maths.context: In One Dose, Two Bodies you give drops of colour to a small glass and to a big pot. The colour is equally strong when the drops and the water grow together.
maths.why_maths: A ratio tells you the dose for any size of body from one dose you already know.

maths.problem: A made-up medicine needs 10 milligrams for each kilogram of body mass. A child has a mass of 25 kilograms and a grown-up 60 kilograms. Find both doses. How many times too strong is the grown-up's dose for the child?
maths.answer: The child needs 250 milligrams and the grown-up 600 milligrams. The grown-up's dose is 2.4 times too strong for the child.
maths.explain: 10 times 25 is 250, and 10 times 60 is 600. 600 divided by 250 is 2.4. So the grown-up's dose is more than twice what the child's body should get.
maths.context: In One Dose, Two Bodies a small glass stands for a child's body and a big pot for a grown-up's. Many real doses are worked out from body mass. The medicine here is made up.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by body mass gives each body its own dose, and dividing shows how wrong a borrowed dose would be.

maths.problem: Burning 1 kilogram of LPG makes about 3 kilograms of carbon dioxide. A full home cylinder holds 14.2 kilograms of LPG. About how much carbon dioxide does one cylinder make? How can the gas weigh more than the fuel?
maths.answer: About 42.6 kilograms. The extra mass is oxygen from the air.
maths.explain: 14.2 times 3 is 42.6. Each carbon atom in the fuel joins with two oxygen atoms from the air. So the carbon dioxide holds the fuel's carbon and also the air's oxygen.
maths.context: In the Fuel Diary you time how long your family's gas stove burns each day. The stove burns LPG from a cylinder.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how much carbon dioxide a home makes, which nobody can see or weigh at the stove.

maths.problem: In Feed the Field, one farmer uses 2 beans every season and another uses 3. In six seasons the rain is heavy twice. Work out each farmer's bags. How many beans does each send to the pond?
maths.answer: The 2-bean farmer keeps 20 bags and sends 2 beans to the pond. The 3-bean farmer keeps 18 bags and sends 6 beans.
maths.explain: With 2 beans: four light seasons give 6 minus 2, which is 4 bags each, so 16. Two heavy seasons give 4 minus 2, which is 2 bags each, so 4. That makes 20, and 2 beans washed away. With 3 beans: every season gives 6 minus 3, which is 3 bags, so 18. One bean goes to the pond every season, so 6.
maths.context: In Feed the Field you are a farmer who chooses how many beans of fertiliser to buy each season. Extra beans wash into a shared pond.
maths.why_maths: Working out both plans shows that more fertiliser gave fewer bags and three times the pollution.

maths.problem: In 100 kilograms of urea there are 46 kilograms of nitrogen. A farmer spreads two 45 kilogram bags. Her crop takes up half of the nitrogen. How many kilograms of nitrogen does the crop not take up?
maths.explain: Two bags are 90 kilograms of urea. 46 hundredths of 90 is 41.4 kilograms of nitrogen. Half of 41.4 is 20.7. So about 20.7 kilograms are left to wash away or escape to the air.
maths.context: In Feed the Field, fertiliser that the crop cannot use washes into the pond. On a real field, a crop often takes up about half of the nitrogen in the urea.
maths.why_maths: The numbers on the bag turn 'some is wasted' into an amount that a farmer can try to cut.

maths.problem: In Three Paints, a child scored the colour that came off: paint A scored 2 dry and 2 wet. Paint B scored 1 dry and 2 wet. Paint C scored 0 dry and 1 wet. Which paint would you choose for a card kept indoors? Which for a pot left in the rain? Explain.
maths.answer: Indoors, paint B or paint C would do. In the rain, only paint C comes close, and even paint C lost a little.
maths.explain: Indoors only the dry score matters. B scored 1 and C scored 0, so both hold far better than A. In rain the wet score matters. A and B both scored 2, so both would wash off. C scored 1, so it is the best of the three, but not yet rainproof.
maths.context: In Three Paints you make three paints from one colour powder. You score how much colour rubs off, dry and wet. These scores are made up.
maths.why_maths: A table with two scores for each paint lets you choose a different winner for a different job.
