how_we_found_out.story: Two hundred years ago, most chemists believed in a 'life force'. They thought that substances of living bodies, such as sugar and urea, could be made only inside a living being. A chemist could take such substances apart, but could never build them. In 1828 a young German chemist, Friedrich Wöhler, was heating a salt called ammonium cyanate. Chemists counted this salt as a mineral substance. White crystals formed. He tested them and found that they were urea, the same substance that kidneys make. He wrote to his teacher, Jöns Jacob Berzelius, that he could make urea without needing a kidney. The old belief did not end that day. But chemists went on to build one substance of living bodies after another. In 1856 William Perkin, aged 18, tried to make the medicine quinine from coal tar. He failed, and found a purple dye. Dye factories grew from his discovery, and medicine factories grew from the dye factories. Today factories make urea from air, natural gas and water, by the million tonnes.
how_we_found_out.who: Friedrich Wöhler in Germany, his teacher Jöns Jacob Berzelius in Sweden, and William Perkin in England
how_we_found_out.when: Wöhler made urea in 1828. Perkin made his purple dye in 1856.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the substances of living bodies can be made only inside a living being, by a life force. Wöhler made urea from a mineral salt. Later chemists made many more such substances.
how_we_found_out.art: A young chemist in clothes of the 1820s holding up a glass dish of white crystals in a small laboratory, with a letter and a quill pen on the bench.

roots.context: In this unit you saw how chemistry makes fertilisers, medicines, fuels and paints. Here we ask what makes one substance a help at one time and a harm at another.

deep_truth.truth: In One Dose, Two Bodies, two drops made the small glass dark and left the big pot pale. The drops were the same, and only the amount of water around them changed. A medicine spreads through a body in the same way, and plant food through the water in soil. So a substance helps or harms depending on its amount and on the size of the body.
deep_truth.habit: We sort substances into good ones and bad ones: medicine and poison, plant food and pollution. The sorting leaves out the amount. Urea feeds a paddy field and kills the fish in the pond below.
deep_truth.evidence: In One Dose, Two Bodies, the pot needed about 20 drops to match the glass with 2. The big pot's dose made a small glass far too dark. In Feed the Field, 2 beans raised the harvest, and the third bean only reached the pond.

three.who_am_i: Scientists estimate that about half the nitrogen in people's bodies today passed through a fertiliser factory. Before that, it was in the air.
three.what_is_life: Every living being takes in substances, and needs each one in an amount that fits their size. Too little starves a body, and too much harms it.
three.what_is_this_world: Air, rock, crude oil and plants are made of the same kinds of atoms as medicines, fuels and paints. A factory only changes which atoms are joined to which.

roots.thread: A nitrogen atom may be in the air one year and in a bag of urea the next. A year later it is in a grain of rice. Then it is in your muscle. It is the same atom each time, with different partners. The same is true of amounts. Urea in the right amount is food for a field. The same urea in the pond is pollution. Many sages taught that everything comes from one source. The science here says something close and plain: fertiliser, medicine and poison are made of the same few kinds of atoms. The joining and the amount make the difference.

teachings.source: Tirukkural 949, in the chapter on medicine
teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar says that a learned healer first weighs three things: the measure of the patient, the measure of the illness and the season. Only then does the healer act.
teachings.link: This is the same finding as One Dose, Two Bodies, written in Tamil about 1,500 years ago or more. The right amount depends on who receives it. The verse is advice to healers, and it was not the result of a measured test.

teachings.source: Paracelsus, Septem Defensiones (Seven Defences), third defence, written in 1538
teachings.teaching: All things are poison, and nothing is without poison. The dose alone makes a thing not a poison.
teachings.link: Paracelsus was a doctor answering people who accused him of giving poisons as medicines. His line is still the first rule of the science of poisons. Modern scientists add that for a few substances, such as lead, no safe dose has been found.

teachings.teaching: To keep filling a bowl to the brim is not as good as stopping in time.
teachings.link: In Feed the Field, the third bean added nothing to the harvest and went into the pond. The text is about how to live. Farmers and doctors have found that the same holds for fertiliser and medicine.

science.text: For almost every substance tested, the effect on a body grows with the dose. Scientists draw this as a curve for each substance, and they use it to set safe limits.
The atoms in factory urea are the same kinds of atoms as those in the urea your body makes. No test can tell the two apart.
Some scientists think that very small doses of some harmful things can do a body good. This idea is called hormesis, and scientists disagree about how often it is true.

other_view.who: Many scientists who study poisons and public health
other_view.view: The line 'the dose makes the poison' can be misused. Factories have used it to say that a little of their waste does no harm. For lead, and for some substances that cause cancer, no safe amount has been found. The same dose also acts differently on a baby before birth, a child and a grown-up. On this view, some substances are simply harmful, and the safest dose of them is none.

practice.title: Three breaths of air
practice.say: Sit still and put one hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly. Four fifths of that breath is nitrogen. It goes in, and it comes out again unchanged. Breathe in again. One fifth is oxygen, and your body keeps a little of it. Breathe a third time. The nitrogen you cannot use from the air reached you another way. It came in your food. Sit quietly for five more breaths.
practice.kid: Sit still. Put a hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly, three times. Most of each breath is nitrogen. Your nitrogen came in your food.

ask: In One Dose, Two Bodies, the same drops were strong in the glass and weak in the pot. Is anything strong or weak by itself?
Urea feeds the paddy field and harms the pond below it. Is urea a good substance or a bad one?
The nitrogen in your body was once in the air, and some of it passed through a factory. Is it yours, the air's or the factory's?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with one hand on her belly, with a faint line drawn from the sky to a factory, to a paddy field, to a plate of rice, to her.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through carefully but have not yet been tried at home. Three Paints (core) needs a colour powder, soft cooked rice, white glue and a piece of carton. It takes about 35 minutes of doing, with 30 minutes of drying in the middle. Start it early and read the story during the wait. The expected result has three parts. The powder with water alone rubs off as dust. The rice paste paint holds when dry and smears when wet. The glue paint holds best. Kolam powder is coarser than chalk and may rub off a little from every paint. Turmeric must not be used, because it stains the card. One Dose, Two Bodies (core) needs two clear glasses of the same size, a pot and food colour or ink. Most families should find a match at about 20 drops. Matching by eye is rough, so any answer from 16 to 24 is good. Drops from a straw differ in size, so let the child practise first. Strong coffee works in place of food colour only if a quarter teaspoon is used for every 2 drops. The Four Finds (core) needs a grown-up to hold the medicine. The Crude Oil Ladder (core) needs only a newspaper, scissors, a candle and petroleum jelly. The paper strips are a model, and the note says so. The Tea Factory needs a grown-up at the stove. The Fuel Diary takes three days. Meals differ from day to day, so only a difference of more than about 10 minutes means anything. The Slow Tablet is hard. A thin dough wall may leak in under a minute, and a thick one may hold for over an hour. Finding the middle is the challenge. Feed the Field was checked by working out every case in the harvest table. Two beans a season gives the most bags on average. No part needs a garden or an animal. Facts to treat with care: the share of the world's food grown with factory nitrogen, about half, is an estimate. The carbon chain lengths for petrol, diesel and wax are rounded ranges. The Tirukkural's date is uncertain. The verses from the Tirukkural, Paracelsus and the Tao Te Ching are given as paraphrases. The three videos have no address yet.
